text: For some professions, definitely, since you can't become a doctor or a lawyer without one. But in fields like design or programming, practical skills and a strong portfolio often count for more than a diploma. I'd say a degree is no longer a guarantee of success, as it used to be. What matters is continuing to learn, whether that's through university, online courses or on-the-job training.

text: There can be many reasons. Sometimes the subject simply doesn't seem relevant to their lives, so they can't see the point. Others are overwhelmed by pressure from parents or exams, which actually reduces their desire to learn. I think motivation improves when students have clear, achievable goals and some control over what they study. A teacher who gives encouragement rather than criticism also makes a huge difference.

text: A balance would be ideal. Academic subjects develop critical thinking and general knowledge, which every citizen needs. Yet most graduates admit they leave school without knowing how to manage money, cook or deal with stress. If schools included a few practical lessons like these, students would be better prepared for adult life. It wouldn't need to come at the expense of maths or literature, just a smarter use of time.

text: I think it'll become far more personalised. Software will probably adapt lessons to each student's pace, so nobody is left behind or held back. Classrooms may also be less central, with more learning happening in blended formats. Still, I doubt teachers will disappear. Their role is likely to shift towards mentoring and motivating, which is something even the smartest technology struggles to do convincingly.
